documents.title: Statement on Responsible and Acceptable Use of Artificial Intelligence
documents.stance_why: The statement sets no stance on student AI use in coursework. It speaks of "responsible and acceptable use", sets data-handling rules, and refers readers to System guidance for students and instructors, so it hands classroom decisions elsewhere (delegates).
documents.summary: Short IT-office statement on responsible and acceptable AI use at UIC. It states principles, data-handling duties for sensitive data and a note that guidance will change, and points to U of I System student and instructor guidance for classroom rules.

units.why: The statement says "UIC recognizes the potential benefits of AI, in enhancing teaching, research, and healthcare", naming benefits without making a rule, so P87 (benefits) fits and P44 (career skill) does not.
units.anchor: UIC recognizes the potential benefits of AI, in enhancing teaching, research, and healthcare

units.why: The passage commits the campus: "We are committed to using AI ethically and in alignment with our guiding principles and our mission". It is an institution-level statement of purpose and principle, hence P56.
units.anchor: We are committed to using AI ethically and in alignment with our guiding principles
units.frag_start: We are committed to using AI ethically
units.policy: UIC commits to using AI ethically and in alignment with its guiding principles and mission.

units.why: "the responsible use of AI requires a multidisciplinary approach, involving collaboration between faculty, IT professionals, researchers, students" states a principle that responsible use needs shared work among groups, which is the institution framework (P56); P88 is about external coalitions and does not apply.
units.anchor: the responsible use of AI requires a multidisciplinary approach
units.policy: UIC holds that responsible use of AI requires a multidisciplinary approach with collaboration between faculty, IT professionals, researchers, students and others.

units.why: "We acknowledge that this technology will evolve, and that continued dialogue is needed" says the guidance is provisional and open to dialogue, which is P54 (revisit regularly).
units.anchor: this technology will evolve, and that continued dialogue is needed
units.policy: UIC acknowledges that this technology will evolve and that continued dialogue is needed.

units.why: "UIC is actively monitoring this topic and is engaging with stakeholders" describes ongoing institutional monitoring and stakeholder engagement; closest is P54, though it is also about current engagement.
units.anchor: UIC is actively monitoring this topic and is engaging with stakeholders
units.frag_start: To that end, UIC is actively
units.policy: UIC is actively monitoring AI and engaging with stakeholders.
units.fit_note: Also states current stakeholder engagement, not only future revision.

units.why: "As a collaborative effort between UIC & U of I System IT Security, Privacy, Risk Leadership" records who developed the listed policies, matching P84 (how and by whom the policy was made).
units.anchor: a collaborative effort between UIC & U of I System IT Security, Privacy, Risk Leadership
units.policy: The listed AI policies were developed as a collaborative effort between UIC and U of I System IT Security, Privacy, Risk Leadership, and others.

units.why: "This statement provides information and policies on the responsible and acceptable use of AI within our UIC Community" sets scope and purpose of the statement, an institution-wide framework (P56).
units.anchor: provides information and policies on the responsible and acceptable use of AI
units.policy: This statement provides information and policies on the responsible and acceptable use of AI within the UIC Community.

units.why: "Please read these in their entirety" directs all readers to read the System-level AI principles and student/instructor guidance, which is a duty to stay informed about current guidance (P102).
units.anchor: Please read these in their entirety.
units.policy: Readers read the listed AI policies and guidance in their entirety.
units.fit_note: Also delegates the actual student and instructor rules to the System documents.

units.why: "should submit a ticket to security@uic.edu" gives a route for entering "high-risk or sensitive data" into an AI tool, a data-protection rule (P50); it is not P65 because it is a user duty and not an institutional review.
units.anchor: who need to enter high-risk or sensitive data into an AI tool or service should
units.policy: Students, staff, faculty and researchers who need to enter high-risk or sensitive data into an AI tool or service should submit a ticket to security@uic.edu and reference the guidance, principles and policies.

units.why: "must have appropriate contracts and data-use agreements in place" requires contracts for high-risk data in any AI solution; this is vendor and data-sharing approval, P65.
units.anchor: must have appropriate contracts and data-use agreements in place
units.policy: High-risk or sensitive data created, stored, or managed in any AI solution must have appropriate contracts and data-use agreements in place.

units.why: "choosing tools and services that exhibit the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST’s) characteristics of trustworthy AI" advises picking trustworthy tools; nearest is P50 (prefer vetted tools) but the criterion is NIST, not university licensing.
units.anchor: choosing tools and services that exhibit
units.frag_start: For uses of AI that are not prohibited
units.policy: For uses of AI that are not prohibited, UIC faculty, staff, students and affiliates can protect themselves and others by choosing tools and services that exhibit NIST characteristics of trustworthy AI.
units.fit_note: Prefers tools meeting NIST trustworthy-AI characteristics, not university-vetted tools.

units.why: "If you discover outdated information ... please provide comments by sending an email to security@uic.edu" invites feedback and flags that material may be dated, which is P54 (feedback invited).
units.anchor: please provide comments by sending an email
units.policy: Some material may be dated; users who find outdated information or have feedback send comments to security@uic.edu.

documents.title: Generative AI resources and guidance for faculty
documents.stance_why: The letter sets no rule on student AI use. It "encourage[s] their responsible use" and points faculty to CATE's example syllabus statements "that you can adapt for your course", leaving the decision to instructors (delegates).
documents.summary: Provost and Health Affairs letter to faculty from September 2023 reminding them of System and campus generative AI guidance. It encourages responsible use, repeats the sensitive-data ticket rule, and points to CATE syllabus statements and workshops.

units.why: "we encourage their responsible use in our academic community" welcomes AI use while adding "responsible"; closest is P02 (permit or encourage), the responsibility condition is the extra.
units.anchor: we encourage their responsible use in our academic community
units.policy: The provost's office encourages responsible use of large language models in the academic community.
units.fit_note: Encouragement is limited to "responsible" use and not tied to a specific activity.

units.why: "it is essential that we are well informed of their benefits and risks" asks faculty to keep informed about AI, matching P102.
units.anchor: it is essential that we are well informed of their benefits and risks
units.frag_end: responsible use in our academic community.
units.policy: It is essential that the academic community is well informed of the benefits and risks of large language models.

units.why: "safeguarding our standards of academic integrity and excellence" explains that the guidance exists to protect integrity while navigating AI; it is the purpose and principle of the guidance (P56) rather than a fairness argument (P95) because no fairness claim is made.
units.anchor: safeguarding our standards of academic integrity and excellence
units.frag_start: The University of Illinois System and the UIC campus
units.policy: The System and campus developed guidance to help faculty and students navigate generative AI while safeguarding standards of academic integrity and excellence.

units.why: "We encourage you to read these documents in their entirety" tells faculty to read the System and campus AI guidance, which is a duty to stay informed (P102).
units.anchor: We encourage you to read these documents in their entirety
units.frag_start: reflects the collaborative effort among UIC
units.policy: Faculty read the listed AI guidance documents in their entirety.

units.why: "collaborative effort among UIC and U of I System leadership in IT security, risk, and privacy to develop guidance" records who made the guidance (P84).
units.anchor: collaborative effort among UIC and U of I System leadership in IT security, risk, and
units.frag_start: reflects the collaborative effort among UIC
units.frag_end: responsible and acceptable use of generative AI.
units.policy: The UIC statement on generative AI reflects collaboration among UIC and U of I System leadership in IT security, risk and privacy.

units.why: "should submit a ticket to security@uic.edu" is the same data rule as in the IT statement, repeated here for faculty, so it is coded as P50 data protection for this document.
units.anchor: who need to enter high-risk or sensitive data into a generative AI tool or service
units.policy: Students, staff, faculty and researchers who need to enter high-risk or sensitive data into a generative AI tool or service should submit a ticket to security@uic.edu.

units.why: "must have appropriate contracts and data-use agreements in place" requires contracts for sensitive data in any generative AI solution (P65).
units.anchor: must have appropriate contracts and data-use agreements in place
units.policy: High-risk or sensitive data created, stored, or managed in any generative AI solution must have appropriate contracts and data-use agreements in place.

units.why: The CATE guide "includes AI usage policy example statements that you can adapt for your course and include in your syllabus", so faculty may adopt a syllabus statement; nearest is P09, though it is optional and not a requirement.
units.anchor: AI usage policy
units.frag_start: The guide includes AI usage policy
units.policy: CATE's Teaching Guide includes AI usage policy example statements faculty can adapt for their course and include in the syllabus.
units.fit_note: Offers syllabus statement templates but does not require a statement.

units.why: "attend an upcoming CATE workshop on Enhancing Teaching and Learning with Generative AI Tools" and the teaching@uic.edu contact are faculty support for learning AI (P63).
units.anchor: Enhancing Teaching and Learning with Generative AI Tools
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to attend CATE workshops on Enhancing Teaching and Learning with Generative AI Tools and may email teaching@uic.edu for guidance on AI in the classroom.

units.why: The Provost’s Leadership Retreat featured "a panel of UIC and UI Health experts" on generative AI, with a recording to view; this is faculty learning support (P63).
units.anchor: a panel of UIC and UI Health experts
units.policy: The Provost's Leadership Retreat featured a panel of UIC and UI Health experts on generative AI, and a recording and presentation are available to faculty.

units.why: "will be updated as new content becomes available, or as content becomes dated" commits the provost website to updating its generative AI resources, P54.
units.anchor: will be updated as new content becomes available, or as content becomes dated
units.policy: Generative AI resources posted on the Provost's website will be updated as new content becomes available or as content becomes dated.

units.why: "drives our approach to using generative AI in responsible, ethical, and appropriate ways, which preserve academic integrity and privacy" states the mission-based principle behind the approach (P56).
units.anchor: using generative AI in responsible, ethical, and appropriate ways, which preserve academic integrity and privacy
units.frag_start: Our commitment to our system mission
units.policy: The university's approach to generative AI is to use it in responsible, ethical and appropriate ways that preserve academic integrity and privacy.

documents.unit: Center for the Advancement of Teaching Excellence (CATE)
documents.title: Teaching Guide: AI Writing Tools
documents.stance_why: The guide states "there is no universal approach" and gives three example syllabus statements (prohibit, limited use, all use) for instructors to adapt, so it sets no stance and lists tiers.
tiers: Permit limited use of AI writing tools
Permit all use of AI writing tools
documents.summary: Teaching-center guide from 2023 on generative AI writing tools. It explains benefits and concerns, gives step-by-step advice and three template syllabus statements, offers strategies to reduce misuse and sample AI activities, and teaches prompting and citation checking.

units.why: "Generative AI systems are software applications that can create text, images, audio, or video in response to prompts" defines generative AI and sets what the guide covers (P61).
units.anchor: Generative AI systems are software applications that can create text, images, audio, or video
units.policy: Generative AI systems are software applications that can create text, images, audio, or video in response to prompts.

units.why: "AI writing tools are one type of generative AI that can support writing tasks by creating human-like text" defines the guide's object, AI writing tools, so P61.
units.anchor: AI writing tools are one type of generative AI that can support writing tasks
units.frag_start: AI writing tools are one type
units.policy: AI writing tools are one type of generative AI that can support writing tasks by creating human-like text.

units.why: "instructors and students should carefully consider how, why, and if they should incorporate them" leaves the decision to instructors and students rather than setting a rule; P04 fits best.
units.anchor: instructors and students should carefully consider how, why, and if they should incorporate them
units.frag_start: Nevertheless, because these tools are still quite new
units.policy: Instructors and students should carefully consider how, why and if they should incorporate AI writing tools into their personal and professional communication.
units.fit_note: Also asks students, not only instructors, to consider whether to use the tools.

units.why: "it is important for instructors to give them opportunities to skillfully engage with the technology" argues students should practice with AI as preparation for their profession, which is P44 (professional skill).
units.anchor: it is important for instructors to give them opportunities to skillfully engage with the technology
units.policy: Instructors give students opportunities to skillfully engage with AI because it will be part of their chosen discipline and prepares them for future professional work.

units.why: "students can also prompt AI writing tools to provide feedback on their writing" names a benefit and a student use; P87 (benefits) fits since it is framed as why to use, not as a rule.
units.anchor: students can also prompt AI writing tools to provide feedback on their writing
units.policy: Students can prompt AI writing tools to provide feedback on their writing, and instructors can use the tools to decrease writer's block.

units.why: "Instructors can utilize these tools to generate initial drafts of many different types of documents including announcements, outlines, and lesson plans" is an instructor use of AI in teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: Instructors can utilize these tools to generate initial drafts of many different types of documents
units.policy: Instructors can use AI writing tools to generate initial drafts of announcements, outlines and lesson plans.

units.why: "AI writing tools can help instructors create content for their courses that exists in multiple formats" names instructor use to adapt course content, P59.
units.anchor: AI writing tools can help instructors create content for their courses that exists in multiple
units.frag_start: AI writing tools can help instructors
units.policy: AI writing tools can help instructors create course content in multiple formats, for example rephrasing complex texts at different reading levels.

units.why: "generative AI can create custom questions that focus on specific topics that can be used for exam preparation or skill development" is AI for practice questions (P14).
units.anchor: generative AI can create custom questions that focus on specific topics
units.frag_start: generative AI can create custom questions
units.policy: Generative AI can create custom questions on specific topics for exam preparation or skill development.

units.why: Translation "can support students working in non-primary languages" is a stated benefit of AI for learners (P87); it is not P18 because no rule on prose versus code is given.
units.anchor: which can support students working in non-primary languages
units.frag_start: Generative AI models can also fulfill
units.policy: Generative AI models can fulfill some language translation tasks, which can support students working in non-primary languages.

units.why: "Text generated by ChatGPT may seem plausible but may actually be incorrect or invented" warns that AI output is unreliable, P31.
units.anchor: Text generated by ChatGPT may seem plausible but may actually be incorrect or invented
units.policy: Text generated by ChatGPT may seem plausible but may be incorrect or invented, including nonexistent citations and incorrect calculations.

units.why: "can result in unequal access for students with different economic resources" names the cost and equity concern (P51).
units.anchor: can result in unequal access for students with different economic resources
units.frag_start: Similar to any other fast-growing technology
units.policy: Some versions of generative AI tools require a fee, which can result in unequal access for students with different economic resources.

units.why: "can amplify systemic, statistical, and human biases" names bias as a concern, P53.
units.anchor: can amplify systemic, statistical, and human biases
units.policy: Large training datasets can amplify systemic, statistical and human biases, and it is important to understand and acknowledge these biases before encouraging students to use AI writing tools.

units.why: "Generative AI models can collect large amounts of personal information" names data privacy risk, P50.
units.anchor: Generative AI models can collect large amounts of personal information
units.policy: Generative AI models can collect large amounts of personal information, and it is not always known how it is used, which can cause data security and privacy issues.

units.why: "instructors should consider their course learning objectives and whether a specific AI writing tool would help their students meet those targets" ties the AI decision to learning objectives (P83).
units.anchor: instructors should consider their course learning objectives and whether a specific AI writing tool
units.policy: Instructors should consider their course learning objectives and whether a specific AI writing tool would help their students meet those targets.

units.why: "there is no universal approach ... you should take into account different factors, including your course's learning objectives" leaves the AI rule to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: While there is no universal approach to utilizing AI writing tools in your classroom
units.frag_start: While there is no universal approach
units.policy: There is no universal approach to AI writing tools in the classroom; instructors take into account course learning objectives, relevant disciplinary skills and their own comfort with the technology.

units.why: "Share with students your personal stance on AI writing tools" asks instructors to explain their own thinking to students, which is P66 (explain and discuss the rules).
units.anchor: Share with students your personal stance on AI writing tools in the classroom.
units.frag_start: Share with students your personal stance
units.policy: Instructors share with students their personal stance on AI writing tools and discuss AI writing tools as part of class norms and expectations.

units.why: "Develop and include an AI usage policy in your syllabus" tells instructors to put a policy in the syllabus, P09, as a recommendation.
units.anchor: Develop and include an AI usage policy in your syllabus.
units.frag_start: Develop and include an AI usage policy
units.policy: Instructors develop and include an AI usage policy in the syllabus reflecting AI-usage expectations in the classroom.

units.why: "Consult page 11 of UIC’s Student Disciplinary Policy, which provides information on Academic Integrity that can be applied to the usage of AI tools" says misuse falls under existing integrity rules (P36).
units.anchor: Academic Integrity that can be applied to the usage of AI tools
units.policy: UIC's Student Disciplinary Policy provides information on Academic Integrity that can be applied to the usage of AI tools.
units.fit_note: Points instructors to the policy without stating that AI misuse is misconduct outright.

units.why: The example statement says "The use of AI writing tools ... is NOT permitted in this course", a template for a ban on AI in the course, so P01.
units.anchor: is NOT permitted in this course
units.frag_start: The use of AI writing tools (including, but not limited to,
units.frag_end: Sudowrite) is NOT permitted in this course.
units.policy: The use of AI writing tools (including ChatGPT, Bard or Sudowrite) is NOT permitted in this course (example syllabus statement).

units.why: "Students who use these tools for class assignments undermine the goals and learning objectives for this course" gives the reason for the ban: AI undercuts learning, P41.
units.anchor: undermine the goals and learning objectives for this course, reducing the effectiveness of instruction
units.policy: Students who use AI writing tools for class assignments undermine the goals and learning objectives of the course, reducing the effectiveness of instruction (example statement).

units.why: "The instructor may submit student writing to an AI writing detector (e.g., GPTZero) at any point" tells students detectors may be used, P40.
units.anchor: The instructor may submit student writing to an AI writing detector (e.g., GPTZero)
units.frag_start: The instructor may submit student writing
units.policy: The instructor may submit student writing to an AI writing detector (e.g., GPTZero) at any point throughout the term (example statement).

units.why: "Any confirmed use of AI writing tools will be treated as cheating" classifies unauthorized use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Any confirmed use of AI writing tools will be treated as cheating.
units.policy: Any confirmed use of AI writing tools will be treated as cheating (example statement).

units.why: "Students are encouraged to use AI writing tools ... to generate ideas for their writing and course work" in the limited-use example welcomes brainstorming, P15.
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to use AI writing tools
units.frag_start: Students are encouraged to use AI writing tools
units.policy: Students are encouraged to use AI writing tools (such as ChatGPT, Bard or Sudowrite) to generate ideas for their writing and course work (example statement).

units.why: "it is expected that all AI-generated content be reviewed, edited, and verified for accuracy before submission" requires verifying AI output (P31).
units.anchor: all AI-generated content be reviewed, edited, and verified for accuracy before submission
units.policy: All AI-generated content is reviewed, edited and verified for accuracy before submission (example statement).

units.why: "you need to cite the specific AI writing tool as a source if you present any significant amount (i.e., more than one sentence) of minimally edited AI-generated text" sets a disclosure rule with a threshold (P24).
units.anchor: you need to cite the specific AI writing tool as a source if you present
units.frag_start: Please note that you need to cite
units.policy: Students cite the specific AI writing tool as a source if they present more than one sentence of minimally edited AI-generated text as their own (example statement).
units.fit_note: Disclosure is required only above a size threshold of more than one sentence of minimally edited text.

units.why: "In order to prepare students for an AI-infused world" gives the preparation reason behind permitting limited use, P44.
units.anchor: In order to prepare students for an AI-infused world
units.policy: AI writing tools are permitted in some ways in order to prepare students for an AI-infused world (example statement).

units.why: "the use of AI writing tools is permitted in this course with no restrictions" is the open template, a permit-by-default rule (P02).
units.anchor: the use of AI writing tools is permitted in this course with no restrictions
units.frag_start: In order to prepare students for AI-assisted work
units.policy: The use of AI writing tools is permitted in this course with no restrictions (example statement).

units.why: "these technologies change at a rapid pace and may require that your policy be updated or clarified regularly" asks instructors to revisit the policy (P54).
units.anchor: may require that your policy be updated or clarified regularly
units.frag_start: Keep in mind that these technologies
units.policy: Because AI technologies change at a rapid pace, the course AI policy may need to be updated or clarified regularly.

units.why: "You may also choose to differentiate your policy for different assignments within the same course" allows assignment-level rules, P04.
units.anchor: You may also choose to differentiate your policy for different assignments within the same course.
units.frag_start: You may also choose to differentiate
units.policy: Instructors may differentiate the AI policy for different assignments within the same course.

units.why: "Test out the tool ... see responses ... for an assignment in your course" advises instructors to try AI on their assignments and adjust them, assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: test out the type of responses AI writing tools may generate for an assignment in
units.frag_start: If you feel comfortable using AI writing tools
units.policy: Instructors who are comfortable with AI writing tools test the responses the tools generate for an assignment and consider adjusting it to promote more authentic work.

units.why: "Make student work collaborative" proposes group work so that "auto-generated text [is] largely irrelevant", an assignment-design response (P35).
units.anchor: Consider adding group work to your courses
units.policy: Instructors consider adding group work, which makes auto-generated text largely irrelevant to the group work completed in class.

units.why: "Scaffold student assignments" with smaller lower-stakes assignments so instructors "see the entire scope of a student's process", assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Segmenting large assignments into smaller, lower-stakes assignments
units.policy: Instructors segment large assignments into smaller, lower-stakes assignments, for example proposal, draft and final work, so they can see the entire scope of a student's process.

units.why: "require students to verify all information in their writing with peer-reviewed sources and cite the evidence" is assignment design to make AI text infeasible (P35).
units.anchor: require students to verify all information in their writing with peer-reviewed sources and cite the
units.policy: For research projects, instructors require students to verify all information with peer-reviewed sources and cite the evidence, including citations and direct links in proposals.

units.why: "Require students to enable track changes throughout assignment components to see their work in progress" collects process evidence from students, P26 (keep drafts), not P40 because the student supplies it.
units.anchor: Require students to enable track changes throughout assignment components
units.frag_start: Require students to enable track changes
units.frag_end: to get credit for solving a problem
units.policy: Instructors require students to enable track changes throughout assignment components and may require them to detail their brainstorming process or show how they arrived at an answer.
units.fit_note: Process evidence is requested to deter AI use, not to disclose AI use.

units.why: "Connect assignments to the classroom" ties prompts to in-class activities so AI output is "less useful", assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: connecting assignment prompts to in-class learning activities
units.policy: Instructors consider connecting assignment prompts to in-class learning activities so that output from AI writing tools is less useful.

units.why: "Make assignments personal, timely, and locally specific" is an assignment-design response to AI (P35).
units.anchor: Make assignments personal, timely, and locally specific.
units.policy: Instructors make assignments personal, timely and locally specific by including self-reflection, personal experiences, local topics or current events.

units.why: "Craft assignments that require higher-level cognitive skills" so students cannot easily submit AI work, assignment design (P35).
units.anchor: Assignments that require students to apply, analyze, or evaluate what they have learned
units.policy: Assignments that require students to apply, analyze or evaluate what they have learned diminish students’ ability to submit AI-generated work as their own.

units.why: "Include multimedia assignment opportunities" such as presentations, videos or podcasts is a format change in response to AI (P35).
units.anchor: Consider including assignments that incorporate multiple ways for students to submit their work
units.policy: Instructors consider assignments that let students submit work as presentations, videos or podcasts.

units.why: "Focus on the benefits of learning ... explaining the purpose of assignments and highlighting the potential drawbacks of relying too heavily on AI" asks instructors to explain reasons to students, P66.
units.anchor: explaining the purpose of assignments and highlighting the potential drawbacks of relying too heavily on
units.frag_start: Encourage students to focus on the advantages
units.frag_end: mere exercises to achieve a grade.
units.policy: Instructors encourage students to focus on the advantages of learning by explaining the purpose of assignments and the drawbacks of relying too heavily on AI, and by emphasizing relevance and personal growth.
units.fit_note: Also aims to build intrinsic motivation, which is prevention of misuse.

units.why: "These tools examine the perplexity ... However, their detection efficacy is not conclusive" says detectors are unreliable (P39).
units.anchor: their detection efficacy is not conclusive
units.frag_end: by AI content detectors (Alimardani and Jane, 2023).
units.policy: Detection efficacy of online AI-content detectors is not conclusive, and other tools can revise AI-generated text to bypass detectors.

units.why: "Check that students aren’t submitting AI content" lists detectors (GPTZero, Originality.ai) that instructors can use to rate the probability of AI generation, P40.
units.anchor: There are online tools that attempt to detect AI-generated content
units.policy: Online tools such as GPTZero, Originality.ai, GLTR.io and OpenAI Classifier attempt to detect AI-generated content by rating its probability of being AI generated.

units.why: "Both factors will impact how effective the strategies described above are in mitigating generative AI reliance or misuse" admits limits on control (P82).
units.anchor: Both factors will impact how effective the strategies described above are
units.policy: Advances in generative AI and student skill will affect how effective the strategies are in mitigating reliance or misuse.

units.why: "Summarize texts. This can help students understand what they just read or serve as a review." is a listed student use for review (P14).
units.anchor: Summarize texts. This can help students understand what they just read or serve as a
units.policy: Instructors can have students use AI writing tools to summarize texts to understand what they read or as a review.

units.why: "Interact in a tutorial-type dialogue and then ask for a summary of their current state of knowledge to share with their instructor" is AI as tutor, plus sharing the result for assessment (P12).
units.anchor: Interact in a tutorial-type dialogue and then ask for a summary of their current state
units.policy: Students interact with an AI writing tool in a tutorial-type dialogue and ask for a summary of their current state of knowledge to share with the instructor or for assessment.
units.fit_note: The dialogue's summary is shared with the instructor for assessment.

units.why: "Prompt generative AI to ask common job interview questions" is a practice use (P14).
units.anchor: Prompt generative AI to ask common job interview questions, provide responses, and then request feedback
units.policy: Students prompt generative AI to ask common job interview questions, provide responses and request feedback on those responses.

units.why: "Provide in-the-moment tutoring and coaching for students" lists AI tutoring as a way instructors can support students (P12).
units.anchor: Provide in-the-moment tutoring and coaching for students.
units.policy: Instructors can use AI writing tools to provide in-the-moment tutoring and coaching for students.
units.fit_note: Framed as an instructor use that supports students.

units.why: "Revise lesson plans, draft learning objectives, or brainstorm new ideas" is an instructor use of AI for teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: Revise lesson plans, draft learning objectives, or brainstorm new ideas.
units.frag_start: Revise lesson plans, draft learning objectives,
units.policy: Instructors can use AI writing tools to revise lesson plans, draft learning objectives or brainstorm new ideas.

units.why: "Automate some teaching tasks, such as writing quiz questions and discussion prompts" is instructor use of AI for course materials (P59).
units.anchor: Automate some teaching tasks, such as writing quiz questions and discussion prompts.
units.policy: Instructors can use AI writing tools to automate some teaching tasks, such as writing quiz questions and discussion prompts.

units.why: "Give students immediate feedback on their writing" lists AI feedback as an instructor use, which is not grading; P101 requires conditions for grading, so P59 is closer.
units.anchor: Give students immediate feedback on their writing.
units.policy: Instructors can use AI writing tools to give students immediate feedback on their writing.
units.fit_note: Feedback to students is named without conditions or human review.

units.why: "Generate model assignment submissions that do not meet assignment guidelines so that students can practice providing appropriate peer feedback" is instructor use for teaching materials (P59).
units.anchor: Generate model assignment submissions that do not meet assignment guidelines
units.policy: Instructors can use AI writing tools to generate model assignment submissions that do not meet guidelines so students can practice peer feedback.

units.why: "help students learn how to craft prompts that garner useful output, evaluate AI text output for quality, accuracy, and originality" says courses can teach AI use as a skill (P44).
units.anchor: help students learn how to craft prompts that garner useful output, evaluate AI text output
units.frag_start: These pedagogical applications of AI writing tools
units.policy: Pedagogical applications of AI writing tools help students learn to craft prompts, evaluate AI output for quality, accuracy and originality, and write essays that combine AI-generated content with their own writing.

units.why: In the Think-Pair-ChatGPT-Pair-Share activity, "Ask students to individually conduct a quick search on ChatGPT" builds AI into a class activity, so P79.
units.anchor: Ask students to individually conduct a quick search on ChatGPT to find more information on

units.anchor: Embrace trial and error: Continuously test and refine your prompts
units.policy: Prompting strategies include adjusting based on feedback, chaining prompts, asking the tool to critique its own output, and continuously testing and refining prompts.

documents.title: Graduate Degree Requirements, Department of Computer Science, 2025
documents.stance_why: The handbook says AI "to improve writing (grammar, fluency), is not forbidden a priori", so AI for editing is allowed with conditions: the student stays responsible, a pre-AI draft is kept, and classes may add limits. Its scope is narrow (editing), so permit with conditions fits better than delegates.
documents.summary: Graduate handbook of the CS department, graduate students only. Two short passages allow generative AI for improving writing, keep the student responsible, allow class-level restrictions, and require a pre-AI draft for the WCP critique.

units.why: "All work the students submit must be their own" is the Non-original work standard that applies to written work, a rule on owning submissions (P29).
units.anchor: All work the students submit must be their own.
units.frag_start: Any unauthorized submission or attempt to submit
units.policy: All work students submit must be their own.
units.fit_note: Rule is general and does not mention AI; it sits right before the AI sentence.

units.why: "The use of generative AI to improve writing (grammar, fluency), is not forbidden a priori" permits AI for editing and fluency in graduate written work (P91).
units.anchor: use of generative AI to improve writing (grammar, fluency), is not forbidden a priori
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI to improve writing
units.policy: Generative AI to improve writing (grammar, fluency) is not forbidden a priori.

units.why: "may be further restricted in specific classes or specific requirement for the degree" lets courses and degree requirements add restrictions, an instructor or unit override (P04); P85 fits less well since it names classes.
units.anchor: may be further restricted in specific classes or specific requirement for the degree
units.frag_start: may be further restricted in specific classes
units.policy: Use of generative AI to improve writing may be further restricted in specific classes or specific requirements for the degree.
units.fit_note: Restrictions are set at class or degree-requirement level, with no named decider.

units.why: "The student is responsible for accuracy and to avoid plagiarism" keeps the student responsible for AI-assisted writing (P29); P31 does not fit since it is not about verifying AI output in general.
units.anchor: The student is responsible for accuracy and to avoid plagiarism.
units.frag_start: The student is responsible for accuracy
units.policy: The student is responsible for accuracy and for avoiding plagiarism when using generative AI to improve writing.
units.fit_note: Also names accuracy, close to P31.

units.why: In the WCP (written critique) rules, "The use of generative AI to improve the writing (grammar, fluency) is not forbidden" repeats the permission for the WCP committee setting (P91).
units.anchor: The use of generative AI to improve the writing (grammar, fluency) is not
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI to improve the writing
units.policy: Generative AI to improve the writing (grammar, fluency) of the WCP critique is not forbidden.

units.why: "the student is responsible for accuracy and to avoid plagiarism" in the WCP rules keeps the student responsible (P29).
units.anchor: the student is responsible for accuracy and to avoid plagiarism
units.frag_start: forbidden, but the student is responsible
units.policy: In the WCP critique, the student is responsible for accuracy and for avoiding plagiarism when using generative AI.
units.fit_note: Also names accuracy, close to P31.

units.why: "An initial draft prior to AI use must be available for review by the committee" requires keeping a pre-AI draft for review, a drafts rule (P26); P90 (work first, then AI) is not stated as a sequencing rule.
units.anchor: An initial draft prior to AI use must be available for review by the committee.
units.frag_start: An initial draft prior to AI use
units.policy: An initial draft prior to AI use must be available for review by the committee.
units.fit_note: The draft is for committee review and implies sequencing (draft before AI).

documents.title: Graduate Degree Requirements, Department of Computer Science, 2023
documents.stance_why: The handbook says students "should not use paraphrasing software (like QuillBot) or AI software for writing (like ChatGPT) or any AI tools for content generation ... unless explicitly allowed", a ban with an explicit-permission exception, so restrict.
documents.summary: Earlier edition (2023) of the CS graduate handbook, graduate students only. It bans AI writing tools and paraphrasing software unless explicitly allowed, exempts spell-checkers, and tells students to ask when in doubt. The 2025 edition relaxed this.

units.why: "All the work you submit must be your own" is the Non-original work standard (P29), directly preceding the AI sentence.
units.anchor: All the work you submit must be your own;
units.policy: All the work students submit must be their own.
units.fit_note: General ownership rule, no AI mention itself.

units.why: "you should not use paraphrasing software (like QuillBot) or AI software for writing (like ChatGPT) or any AI tools for content generation ... unless explicitly allowed" bans AI for writing and content generation unless permitted, so P19 (do not have AI produce submitted work); P06 does not fit as it is not about a silent syllabus.
units.anchor: you should not use paraphrasing software (like QuillBot) or AI software for writing
units.frag_start: you should not use paraphrasing software
units.policy: Students should not use paraphrasing software (like QuillBot), AI software for writing (like ChatGPT) or any AI tools for content generation, unless explicitly allowed to do so.
units.fit_note: Bans AI writing tools and paraphrasing software, with an explicit-permission exception.

units.why: "(spell-checkers are allowed)" exempts spell-checkers from the ban, P100.
units.anchor: (spell-checkers are allowed)
units.frag_start: or any AI tools for content generation
units.policy: Spell-checkers are allowed.

units.why: "unless explicitly allowed to do so" makes AI use depend on explicit permission: the default is no, which is the fallback rule P06.
units.anchor: unless explicitly allowed to do so
units.frag_start: you should not use paraphrasing software
units.policy: AI use for writing and content generation is not permitted unless explicitly allowed.
units.fit_note: Written as an exception to a general ban on the tools rather than as a rule for silent syllabi.

units.why: "If in doubt about the specific tool, ask." tells students to ask before using an uncertain tool (P10).
units.anchor: If in doubt about the specific tool, ask.
units.frag_start: If in doubt about the specific tool,
units.policy: If in doubt about the specific tool, students ask.

units.why: In the WCP rules, "students should not use paraphrasing software (like QuillBot) or AI software for writing (like ChatGPT) or any AI" repeats the ban for the critique, P19.
units.anchor: students should not use paraphrasing software (like QuillBot) or AI software for writing
units.frag_start: students should not use paraphrasing software
units.policy: Students should not use paraphrasing software (like QuillBot), AI software for writing (like ChatGPT) or any AI tools for content generation in the WCP critique.
units.fit_note: Applies to the WCP written critique; spell-checkers are allowed.

units.why: "All the work submitted must be the student's own" in the WCP rules is the ownership rule (P29).
units.anchor: All the work submitted must be the student's own;
units.policy: All the work submitted in the WCP must be the student's own.
units.fit_note: General ownership rule, no AI mention itself.

units.why: "(spell-checkers are allowed). If in doubt about the specific tool, ask." in the WCP rules repeats the spell-checker exemption and the advice to ask (P10).

units.policy: In the WCP critique, spell-checkers are allowed, and students ask if in doubt about a specific tool.
